accounts.name: Eastern Counties Police Alliance
accounts.official_story: Rollout under way. 4 forces, 35 docks, 300-dock framework tender in preparation.

facts.text: We're flying all the time.
14 of 18 docks flew last month, mostly patrol support and missing-person searches.
Six officers who also do other duties. Overtime is the main cost. Scaling to 30 docks needs nine more trained operators and shift cover.
Tarn Valley's data protection officer has not signed off. Norwold's chief constable is cautious after a local privacy row.
Only Westmere and Metro Central fly operationally. Tarn Valley has never flown a live mission and Norwold only trains.
All four forces are keen.
The alliance has the budget.
There is no pooled budget. Each force funds from its own budget and each chief finance officer must approve a call-off.
A 300-dock framework tender, spec being finalised.
The tender specification locks soon (see Deadlines). It has no costed operating model, and nobody has agreed who would fly 300 docks.
Westmere's stadium project is a 30-dock opportunity.
The superintendent thinks 30 docks is unrealistic with current staffing. Nobody has asked her.
A helicopter hour costs the force about 1,500 pounds all-in.
He has no comparable drone figure because overtime for drone operators is not tracked separately. He could pull it in a week.
His chief finance officer will sign a call-off only with a cost per flight set against helicopter hours.
A force's call-off needs its own finance sign-off. The alliance cannot commit them.
Metro Central bids in the autumn finance round. That window closes soon (see Deadlines).
Two missing-person finds in under 12 minutes against about 40 for the helicopter. These are anecdotes. Nobody has compared cost per flight.
We are working through the assessment and it is not finished.
It cannot be signed until we receive the data-flow documents we asked the FlytBase support desk for four months ago. Nobody replied.
With data flows, retention periods, video storage location and access controls I can finish in three weeks. Norwold is waiting to copy my assessment.
The Tarn Valley ticket asking for data-flow documents was logged four months ago and never answered. It sits in the support queue unassigned.
Engineering can produce the data-flow pack (flows, retention, video storage location, access controls) in a week, with the CSM owning the ask: sending it, chasing it, answering the DPO.

accounts.name: Aldermoor Industrial Group
accounts.official_story: ROI proven. 15 plants, 14 docks installed, 13 flying. Case study for 40-plant sister company in preparation.

facts.text: It's useful at night.
The dock flies nightly, but the plant's guard contractor does not act on drone alerts because their contract does not cover it. Alerts go to her phone.
Stefan's deputy, not Stefan, set up the Plant 7 dock and most of the others. He is the one who knows how a rollout is actually done.
She wrote an informal checklist: night patrol routes and alert response. Nobody asked for it and she would share it.
I hear Plant 11 never uses theirs. Their manager sees it as head office's toy and the network there is poor.
The rollout template lives mostly in his deputy's head. The deputy leaves soon (see Deadlines), and nothing is written down.
ROI is proven, about 1.2 million euros a year saved.
The figure is his own spreadsheet of guard patrol hours the drones could replace. No guard contract has been reduced and finance has booked no saving.
Thirteen of fifteen plants are flying.
Four plants fly regularly. Nine only log test flights. Plant 15 has no dock.
Plants pay a share of the security budget. Several managers resent paying for equipment they did not choose.
Plants 11 to 14 have weak links and he had no part in the installs.
A network segmentation project starts in four months and will cut the docks' connectivity unless exceptions are planned. Nobody has told him.
He can give two days of a network engineer to build a pilot plan if asked with specifics.
Security costs are charged to plants through an annual allocation. The drones added cost and she sees no reduction in any guard contract. Nobody has shown her the 1.2 million figure.
She would accept ROI built on measured changes: guard contract renewals (three renew within four months), the insurance premium and incident losses.
The 40-plant sister company is not her budget and she has no view on it.
Every number comes from his spreadsheet and he has not shown it to finance.
The insurer cut premiums by 6% across nine plants, about 180,000 euros a year, citing the drone patrols. It is the only hard financial benefit and nobody in security asked him.
The insurer's review is in five months. Consistent flight logs by plant would extend the discount, and plants with idle docks put it at risk.
The plant is charged an annual allocation it did not choose. She would still keep the dock after two attempted break-ins were deterred, which is anecdotal.

accounts.name: Kestrel Estates
accounts.official_story: 1 dock paid, 0 flying. Waiting on go-live.

facts.text: Everyone here is excited. We are just waiting to go live.
A local installer put the dock in, then moved on. He no longer answers calls.
Power and network were tested at install, but no test flight was done because there was no certified pilot on site.
Nobody at the estate holds a drone pilot certificate. Dana assumed the system flies itself once switched on.
The property insurance requires any new aerial equipment to be notified before use. The dock is not declared.
What the estate needs is night patrol of the two entrances. The sales pitch was about mapping the whole estate, which they do not need.
Any spend beyond the original purchase needs a vote of the residents' board, which meets on the first Monday of each month.
Some residents already ask why they paid for a drone that has never flown.
The south entrance was raised at install but never assessed for coverage.
If it works at the north gate, Dana would like a second dock for the south entrance.
